newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban town falls, another attacked.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban town falls, another attacked.

text.p: Forces of the ousted Afghan government have taken the front-line headquarters town of the purist Islamic Taleban and launched an assault on another on the road south to Kabul, Afghan sources said on Sunday.
They also said guerrilla attacks staged south of the front line by former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had spread to new areas north of Kabul.
The town of Jabal-os-Saraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains fell on Saturday and Masood hit Charikar, a 30-minute drive to the south, on Sunday, they said.

The fall of Jabal-os-Saraj is a major setback for the Taleban, who pursued Masood north after taking Kabul just two weeks ago and bottled up his forces in the Panjsher valley, which begins near the town.

They were unable to penetrate the narrow gorge into the Panjsher and on Tuesday Masood launched a counter-attack in the Salang Pass, then orchestrated a series of guerrilla strikes well behind the front lines.
"Yes, Jabal-os-Saraj has fallen. It fell on Saturday evening," one source told Reuters. "They attacked Charikar early this morning."
The Taleban in Kabul strenuously denied reports that Jabal-os-Saraj, their front line headquarters for both the Salang and Panjsher valley fronts, had fallen.

But the sources said Taleban forces had retreated from Jabal-os-Saraj to Charikar and fighting was still going on in the town late on Sunday afternoon, with Masood loyalists staging hit-and-run attacks from inside houses.
Masood's mostly ethnic Tajik forces have struck in and around Charikar over the last three days.
People in the mostly Tajik town said earlier in the week the largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban had been rounding up young men suspected to fomenting opposition.
Masood commanders say people of the town had joined nn the fight against the Taleban and that it was expected to fall soon.

The charismatic former military chief, who won an outstanding reputation as a guerrilla general in the 1980s when the Soviet army backed a communist government in Kabul, has also orchestrated guerrilla attacks even nearer Kabul.

They cut the main road north remained cut about 15 km (nine miles) north of the Kabul valley and Taleban forces going to and from Charikar, a 90-minute drive from Kabul, had to take a looping side-road that joins the main highway near Charikar.
But that, too, was closed to cvilian traffic on Sunday and the sources said Masood's guerrillas had moved into hills south of Bagram, the government's main airbase 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.

Masood has hit the airbase which shells and mortars repeatedly over the past two days and the Taleban have responded with bombing raids on his suspected positions in the village of Bagram next to the base, witnesses said.
The attacks, reminiscnnt of his tactics in the 1980s have clearly rattled the Taleban and the sources said fighters were now going into villages looking for guerrillas and arms.
The Taleban have who struck back from the main road from Kabul with tank fire and multiple rocket launchers and saxy they have contained them in that area.
But, in sharp contrast to genial conversations with reporters earlier, Taleban on the road have become agressive.

Veteran Afghan watchers in Kabul said that was a sure sign the tide had turned against the Taleban north of Kabul, but that it was unlikely Masood could retake the city without the backing of northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum.
He signed a miltiary pact with the Tajik chief earlier this week, promising to help him unless fighting stopped.
"But Masood has suprised us before and he might again," said one Afghan watcher.
Taleban sources in Pakistan said the Islamic militia had rounded up at least 300 suspected Masood supporters in villages between Bagram and Charikar in the past two days.
They said about 2,000 fresh Taleban fighters had moved to frontlines north of Kabul since Friday, including 600 from Nangarhar province and 1,350 from Paktiya province, both in eastern Afghanistan.
The Paktiya contingent included about 300 men loyal to a renowned guerrilla commander named Maulvi Jalaluddin Haqani.

A spokesman in Islamabad for ousted prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar said he was not a party to the anti-Taleban mutual defence pact signed last week by Dostum, Masood and a faction leader Karim Khalili in the north.
He said Hekmatyar remained prime minister and his forces were fighting the Taleban on the ground.
